title: To be let go
hookLine: the second truth's task is to be abandoned (SN 56.11)

cards: A brahmin named Unnabha once came to the Buddha's attendant, Ananda, with what sounded like a trap. You monks, he said, live the holy life to abandon desire. But how?
You'd need desire to get rid of desire. That's a circle. It's a good question, and plenty of people ask it today: if Buddhism says let go of wanting, isn't wanting to let go just more wanting?
Ananda had an answer, and it involved a walk to a park.

teach.b: In the first sermon, each truth has a task. Dukkha is to be understood. Its cause, craving, is pahātabba: to be abandoned, given up, let go.
Not studied forever, not managed, not fed in smaller portions. Put down.
That sounds harsh until you hear Ananda, in the Connected Discourses, book fifty-one. He asks the brahmin: earlier, did you have the desire to come to this park? Yes.
And now that you've arrived, has that desire died down? Yes. It's the same with a monk, Ananda says.
He has the desire to reach the goal, and when he reaches it, that desire falls away by itself. So not all wanting is the same.
In Pali there's taṇhā, yesterday's thirst, and there's chanda, a wish to do or reach something, which can be wholesome.

teach.h: A GOOD WISH ENDS ON ARRIVAL.
teach.b: The path uses a good wish the way you use a boat, until the crossing's done. And letting go, in the suttas, isn't usually a single dramatic act.
It's more like a hand slowly opening. You see the thirst, and what it costs.
You feel it pull, and you don't follow, once, and then again, and each time it loosens a little. That's why the task is a verb that keeps going.
Craving isn't an enemy to be hated; hating it would just be the third thirst again, the push to make it vanish. It's a weight you discover you don't have to carry.

how: Buddhists in many schools practice letting go through small renunciations, such as keeping extra precepts on observance days, giving things away, and noticing cravings in meditation without following them.

o: to be let go, given up

games.q: match the pieces of today's teaching.
p: the brahmin who asked the riddle
answered with a walk to a park
a wish that can be wholesome

s: Buddhism says every kind of wanting is bad
Ananda shows a wholesome wish, like wanting to reach the park, that falls away on arrival.
the first sermon gives craving the task of being abandoned
its task is pahātabba: to be let go.
the way to let go of craving is to hate it
hating it is just another push; letting go is more like a hand slowly opening.

games.q: you're Ananda. a brahmin says: you need desire to get rid of desire, so your path is a circle. what do you say?
o: ask whether his wish to come to the park ended when he arrived.
games.why: Ananda points out that the wish to reach the park died down on arrival; the wish for the goal falls away when the goal is reached.

practice: Let one small want come up, something to eat, to check, to fix, to be, and feel where it sits in the body, maybe a lean forward or a tightness in the chest.
Don't argue with it; on an out-breath, let the hand of the mind open a little, as if setting something down on a table. If the want comes back, that's fine: set it down again.

wordCard.voice: Pahātabba. To be abandoned, given up, let go: the task the first sermon gives to craving, a hand slowly opening rather than a single dramatic act.

orig.note: Pali pahātabba: to be abandoned or given up, the task the first sermon gives craving.

carryVoice: Your line: let it go. A good wish can carry you there, then fall away on arrival. Day three hundred thirty-eight, done.
